title: Nabi Khan and Ghani Khan
hookLine: two Pathan brothers carried the Guru in disguise as a holy man through enemy lines

lines: A PALANQUIN ON A WATCHED ROAD.
cards: A road patrolled by soldiers. Coming down it, a palanquin, a covered seat carried on poles, with a holy man inside dressed in blue. Two Pathan men are carrying it, with a few others walking alongside.
The soldiers stop them. Who's this? A holy man, the brothers say, a pir, on his way.
They are calm. They are Muslims, telling the soldiers what soldiers would expect to hear. And inside the palanquin sits the man those soldiers are hunting: Guru Gobind Singh.
Today: Nabi Khan and Ghani Khan.

teach.b: After Chamkaur, the Guru made his way through the night, alone for a time, to the forest near Machhiwara. Tradition says that's where a few of his Sikhs found him again, and where help came from an unexpected direction.

Nabi Khan and Ghani Khan were Pathan brothers, horse dealers, who tradition says had sold horses to the Guru in better days and knew him. Now he was a hunted man, and helping him was dangerous. They helped anyway.

teach.h: THE PIR OF UCH, IN BLUE.
teach.b: The Guru would be dressed in blue robes, as a Muslim holy man, a pir. Tradition says they called him the Pir of Uch, a holy man from a faraway town.
They lifted him in a palanquin and carried him on their shoulders through countryside where soldiers were searching. When questioned, they held to their story.
If the soldiers had seen through it, the brothers could have paid with their lives. They weren't Sikhs. No one could have demanded this of them.
They had known him, they trusted him, and when his life was in danger they put their own on the line.
When they parted, tradition says, the Guru gave them a hukamnama, a letter thanking them, so their service would be remembered. And it is.
Sikhs tell this story with deep gratitude, in the same thread as Pir Budhu Shah a few days ago and the Nawab of Malerkotla, whom we'll meet soon.
Brothers of another faith, carrying the Guru on their shoulders.

how: Sikhs remember Nabi Khan and Ghani Khan in tellings of the Guru's escape after Chamkaur, and the story is told at Machhiwara, where the memory of the Guru's stay is kept.

o: two horse dealers who sold the Guru's horses to his enemies
two Muslim brothers who carried the Guru past soldiers

games.q: out of the forest — tap the pairs.

s: they were Muslims, Pathans, who had known the Guru and chose to help him.
the Guru was disguised as a Muslim holy man
tradition says he wore blue and was carried as the Pir of Uch.

games.q: you're Nabi Khan. soldiers stop your palanquin and ask who's inside. what do you do?
o: tell them the truth and hope for mercy.
hold calmly to the story: a holy man on his way.
games.why: tradition says the brothers held to their story and carried the Guru through, and he later thanked them with a letter.

practice: Think of someone more exposed right now than you are: someone being talked about, someone new and alone, someone whose job or reputation is on the line.
Ask what it would cost you to stand a little closer to them, and find one small way to carry part of their weight, the way two brothers once carried a palanquin.

wordCard.voice: Pathan brothers. Nabi Khan and Ghani Khan, who, tradition says, carried Guru Gobind Singh past the soldiers, disguised as a holy man. Today's word.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: Uch da Pir, the holy man of Uch, the Guru's disguise.

carryVoice: Your line: brothers of another faith. They held to their story, and he got through. Day eight hundred twenty-four, done.
